evidence: Phaedr. 3.19.1–2: parāre cēnam jussus est mātūrius
terms.comment: The everyday word: cēnam parāre, to get dinner ready. With an infinitive, to get ready to do, to set about it (cingere parat, Liv. 1.38.6).

evidence: Varro RR 1.37.4: prīmō praeparandum, secundō serendum

terms.gloss: prepare with care (a meal, a wedding)
evidence: Ter. Ad. 901: in apparandō cōnsūmunt diem
Ter. Ad. 966: apparāre dē diē convīvium
terms.comment: Lewis & Short: “to prepare or make ready for something (esp. with effort, care, expense)”. See organise.

phrases.latin: in Tusculānum nōs ventūrōs putāmus aut Nōnīs aut postrīdiē. ibi ut sint omnia parāta
phrases.english: We expect to reach Tusculum on the Nones or the day after. See that everything is ready there.

phrases.latin: Quandō vīs venī, parāta rēs erit. — Properā modo.
phrases.english: Come whenever you like: it’ll be ready. — Just hurry.

phrases.latin: Aesōpus dominō sōlus cum esset familia, parāre cēnam jussus est mātūrius.
phrases.english: Aesop, the only slave his master had, was told to get dinner ready earlier than usual.
